column3: Repeats the "who is better than Allah" comparison, grounding 2:138's divine superlative in His judgment.
Opens the immediate lineage passage with divine favor, supplying its inherited-community setting.
Connects goodness to the believers' recompense, but not to divine imprint or worship.
Joins the best speech to calling to Allah, righteous action, and Muslim self-identification.
Places the surrounding Abrahamic passage in a purified house of embodied worship.
States exclusive worship of Allah, directly clarifying the closing allegiance in 2:138.
Its shared Lord, accountable deeds, and sincere devotion immediately extend 2:138.
Rejects imposed communal labels in favor of Abraham's upright way, sharpening the contrast in 2:138.
Shows separation from competing worship, but adds little beyond the exclusive-devotion theme.
Frames shared revelation and one God through a collective declaration of submission.
Adds a nearby warning of personal accountability without developing the verse's identity or worship claim.
Uses beauty for lasting reward rather than for Allah's formative distinction.
Defines a durable incompatibility between the speaker's worship and the audience's worship.
Abraham and Ishmael pray for themselves and their descendants to be wholly surrendered to Allah.
Provides the Qur'an's concrete use of sibgh as a coloring substance, illuminating the imagery without fixing its meaning.
Presents inherited allegiance as worship of one God and submission, directly within the local sequence.
Connects Abrahamic leadership and covenant to testing, while excluding injustice from the covenant.
Relates excellence to recompense for beneficent people, not to the focal comparison or worship.
Reinforces the worship divide already supplied by 109:3 without adding a distinct dimension.
Links the Abrahamic community to recitation, teaching, wisdom, and purification.
Makes exclusive worship portable across place, broadening the allegiance stated in 2:138.
Declares undivided acceptance of prophetic revelation together with submission to Allah.
Explicitly commends Abraham's way and contrasts turning from it with righteous standing.
Mentions worshipers and their objects but does not itself articulate the focal allegiance.
Affirms Allah's sufficiency for His servant, a secondary support for exclusive reliance.
Continues Abraham's local prayer and distinguishes faith from unbelief, but is not chiefly about the focal claim.
Has Abraham call his people to worship Allah and be mindful of Him.
Shows divine choice overriding human status expectations, only indirectly relevant to divine designation.
Condenses Abraham's response to Allah's command into direct submission to the Lord of all worlds.
States worship of Allah as the purpose of jinn and humankind.
Uses worship language in a claim of human domination rather than Allah-directed devotion.
Immediately supplies the comprehensive confession of revelation and collective submission preceding 2:138.
Concerns the reward of those who do good rather than Allah's dye or worship identity.
Associates faith and righteous action with divine provision, but does not clarify the focal formulation.
Keeps the local Abrahamic house-building and acceptance context in view.
Uses goodness for companionship among the favored, only tangentially related.
Calls Allah's book the best discourse and describes guidance, but not the focal image or allegiance.
Immediately sets shared faith as guidance and refusal as schism before the divine-dye declaration.
Describes a servant granted mercy and knowledge, with no close link to the focal themes.
Most closely parallels 2:138: the best religion is self-surrender to Allah, beneficence, and Abraham's way.
Makes the chosen religion an inherited charge to remain in submission until death.
Treats Allah's provision for servants, a peripheral support for dependence.
Defines excellence as answering evil with what is better, a secondary ethical expression of divine formation.
Follows 2:138 by rejecting later sectarian claims over Abraham and the patriarchs.
Identifies Noah as a believing servant without adding a distinct reading.
Attributes favor to Allah, but supplies no further connection.
Identifies Abraham as a believing servant, a limited corroboration of the local Abrahamic frame.
Contrasts calling on a false deity with abandoning Allah as the best Creator.
Offers Abraham's community as a model of disavowing worship besides Allah and returning to Him.
Addresses punishment for wrongdoing without a meaningful connection to the focal verse.
Identifies two messengers as believing servants, but adds no specific focal clarification.
States Allah has no partner and joins that exclusive allegiance to being among those who submit.
Restates Abraham's good example, though it largely duplicates the preceding parallel.
Combines steadfast invitation, shared lordship, separate deeds, and return to Allah in a close parallel to 2:139.
Challenges the premise that alleged objects of worship participate in that worship.
Denies protectors besides Allah but does not materially clarify the focal wording.
Identifies Elijah as a believing servant without adding a distinct link.
States Allah's guidance and might without a focused connection.
Names Zachariah as Allah's servant, only broadly resonant with devotion.
Expresses ongoing refusal to worship what others worship, complementing the worship contrast.
Uses beauty descriptively without a meaningful relation to divine dye or worship.
Pairs surrender of oneself to Allah with beneficence and secure recompense.
States a prophet's call to worship Allah alone and practice mindfulness.
Names Allah without contributing a discernible focal connection.
Has Abraham publicly dissociate himself from what his father and people worship.
Addresses lack of protection from Allah's judgment, not the focal themes.
Uses a dual form of good outcomes in a conflict setting, only lexically related.
Discusses misguidance and hypocrisy without a focused contribution.
Describes provision and resurrection for servants, with no close interpretive link.
Speaks of Allah increasing goodness from a good deed, a remote ethical association.
Calls the messenger Allah's servant in a narrative setting, without clarifying 2:138.
Contrasts good and bad intercession, not the verse's divine coloration or worship.
Exposes the absence of the things once worshiped, testing rival devotion.
Makes worship of Allah alone the source of extensive beneficence toward others.
Calls return to Allah and the messenger the better resolution, only indirectly related to the superlative.
Concerns communal change and divine decree without a specific focal link.
Shows wrong being replaced by good through forgiveness, a secondary transformation motif.
Relates beneficence and mindfulness to reward after hardship, not the focal identity.
Connects worship of Allah with grateful use of His good provision.
Links doing good, mindfulness, and endurance to reward, but is not close to the focal claim.
Contrasts perceived good work with misdirected effort, a limited caution about appearances.
Sets human worship within universal prostration to Allah while distinguishing those liable to punishment.
Affirms Allah's exclusive divinity and His most beautiful names.
Commands doing good and relates it to Allah's love for beneficent people.
Affirms the truth of revelation and Allah's awareness of servants without a close link.
Directly joins exclusive worship of Allah to concrete excellence toward parents.
Has Abraham interrogate inherited objects of worship, challenging their assumed authority.
Commands Allah's servants to speak what is best, extending excellence into communal conduct.
Portrays alleged worshiped beings as repudiating that worship, exposing its false relation.
Places exclusive worship, beneficence, good speech, and covenant within Israel's inherited obligation.
Shows repentance and mercy, without a direct contribution to the focal verse.
States worship of Allah with religion made sincere for Him alone.
Promises Allah's mighty help without a meaningful focal connection.
Commands prostration to Allah and worship, making the verse's closing allegiance bodily explicit.
Places prophetic revelation and divine guidance against religious dispute, a broader unity context.
Speaks of accepting the best of deeds and overlooking evil, not divine dye or worship.
Addresses consequences of wrongdoing and prohibition of good things without a focused link.
States personal moral consequence and divine justice, only broadly connected to servant accountability.
Names Adam, Noah, Abraham's family, and Imran's family as divinely chosen, supporting lineage context.
Combines patience, repelling evil with good, and spending, a secondary ethical parallel.
States exclusive collective worship of Allah and dependence on Him in the Qur'an's opening prayer.
Provides the local principle that each community bears its own deeds, before the competing-label claims.
Closes the local passage with the same personal accountability after the correction of lineage claims.
Contrasts mere directional affiliation with substantive faith, worship, and righteousness.
Identifies submission as the religion with Allah, directly framing the collective declaration in 2:138.
Denies later communal labels for Abraham and identifies him as upright and surrendered to Allah.
Defines nearness to Abraham through following him, the Prophet, and faith rather than inherited labels.
Commands following Abraham's upright way after affirming Allah's truthfulness.
Commands believers not to die except in submission, closely paralleling the Abrahamic charge in 2:132.
Calls the People of the Book to worship Allah alone and reject partners.
Describes Allah's completion and approval of the religion and His choice of submission for the community.
Locates revealed law within a divine test and directs communities to compete in good deeds rather than collapse difference into rivalry.
Sets Abraham's face toward the Creator as upright and dissociated from association.
Names the straight, upright religion as Abraham's way and denies association.
Makes prayer, sacrifice, life, and death wholly for Allah, expanding exclusive worship into total allegiance.
Commands upright orientation and sincere religion for Allah at every place of worship.
Contrasts human religious authorities with worship of the one God and His exclusive divinity.
Commands setting one's face toward the upright religion and avoiding association.
Portrays Joseph's inherited Abrahamic way as refusal to associate anything with Allah.
Joins Allah's sole judgment to His command that He alone be worshiped, calling this the upright religion.
States the command to worship Allah and not associate partners with Him.
Makes worship of the Lord a continuing practice rather than a merely asserted identity.
Portrays Abraham as a devoted community, upright before Allah, and free of association.
Commands following Abraham's upright way and again excludes association.
Unites one-God revelation, righteous work, and refusal to associate anyone in worship of the Lord.
Pairs Allah's lordship with the command to worship Him as the straight path.
Directly commands worship of Allah and prayer in remembrance of Him.
Gives the shared prophetic message: no deity but Allah, so worship Him.
Names the believers one community under one Lord and commands worship of Him.
Calls for striving for Allah, identifies the Abrahamic religion, and names the community Muslim.
Links upright religion to Allah's originating pattern in humanity, the closest Qur'anic parallel to divine formative identity.
Commands worship of Allah while making religion sincere for Him.
Reserves pure religion for Allah and rejects rival mediating allegiances.
Restates the command to worship Allah with religion made sincere for Him.
Connects the prescribed religion of Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus and forbids division within it.
Completes Abraham's dissociation by affirming allegiance to the One who created him and guides him.
Makes Abraham's monotheistic declaration an enduring word among his descendants.
Combines exclusive worship, sincere religion, uprightness, prayer, and almsgiving as the established religion.
Affirms Allah's absolute oneness, the doctrinal ground of worship directed to Him alone.
